sections.h2: Does Ohio charge an estate tax?
sections.html:
No. The Ohio Department of Taxation reports that House Bill 153 repealed the state estate tax for every estate with a date of death in 2013 or later. House Bill 110 of the 134th General Assembly then added a sunset for the older estates: nothing is owed on property first discovered after December 31, 2021, or on property found earlier but never disclosed or reported by that date.

So an Ohio family selling an inherited house does not file a state estate tax return before closing. The Department also says it has dropped the requirement for ET 12, 13 and 14 release forms before a decedent's assets move to another person, and it asked county auditors and banks to stop forwarding them.

sections.h2: Could the federal estate tax reach an Ohio estate?
sections.html:
Only a very large one. For deaths in 2026 the IRS lists $15,000,000 as the basic exclusion amount, raised by Public Law 119-21, which was signed July 4, 2025. A single house rarely comes near that line, so for most families the federal return does not set the timeline.

The IRS adds two points. An estate that does not have to file a federal return should skip Form 8971, and the estate of someone survived by a spouse may elect to pass unused exclusion to that spouse on a timely filed return.

sections.h2: Who signs the deed when an inherited Ohio house is sold?
sections.html:
Usually the executor or administrator, under the supervision of the probate court that serves the decedent's home county. Ohio's land-sale procedure for executors, administrators and guardians runs from R.C. 2127.01 through 2127.43, and an executor whose will grants a power of sale may follow the will instead.

Smaller estates may not need full administration. Under R.C. 2113.03 the court can release an estate from administration at $35,000 in assets or under, or up to $100,000 when a surviving spouse takes everything. The order can direct delivery of personal property and transfer of real property, and the court may appoint a commissioner to sign the conveyance papers. A buyer who pays value in good faith gets the same protection from unsecured creditors that administration would give.

  • Ask the probate clerk whether the estate fits a release or needs letters of authority.
  • Gather the death certificate, the will, and the vesting deed.
  • Order a title search early so liens surface before a buyer finds them.

sections.h2: What changes if the owner recorded a transfer on death affidavit?
sections.html:
Title may already sit with the named beneficiary. R.C. 5302.22 lets an owner sign a verified transfer on death designation affidavit and record it with the county recorder before death. At the owner's death, title vests in the beneficiaries the affidavit names.

The affidavit needs neither payment nor delivery to work, and the recorder charges the deed fee and indexes it under the owner's name. Heirs who suspect a parent signed one should ask the recorder to search that name. Knowingly false statements in the affidavit are falsification under R.C. 2921.13.

sections.h2: What tax do heirs face when they sell an inherited Ohio house?
sections.html:
The IRS measures gain from the heir's basis, which for inherited property generally equals the fair market value at the date of death. Estates that elected the alternate valuation date use that figure, and farm or business land can use special-use valuation. Publication 551 says an heir who received no Schedule A (Form 8971) from the executor can rely on the appraised date-of-death value used for state inheritance or transmission tax purposes.

That makes an early appraisal worth ordering. Keep it with the estate papers so the tax preparer can apply it to the final price.

On the transfer tax, R.C. 322.02 caps any county levy at thirty cents for each hundred dollars of value, charged to the seller named in the deed and paid at the auditor's office before recording. Ask the county auditor which rate the house falls under.

sections.h2: Can an heir challenge the county's value of the house?
sections.html:
An owner can. R.C. 5715.19 sends a valuation complaint to the county auditor, with a filing deadline of March 31 of the following tax year unless first-half collection closes later. The county board of revision decides it, and the statute limits repeat complaints on one parcel within the same interim period unless something changed, such as an arm's length sale, a casualty loss or a substantial improvement.

A date-of-death appraisal can back up a complaint when the county figure looks high. The auditor's office can say which tax year a new filing would cover.

sections.h2: What will a buyer and title company ask the estate to provide?
sections.html:
Expect requests for proof of who has authority to sign, because a title company will not insure a deed it cannot trace. For an estate in administration that means the executor's or administrator's letters of authority from the probate court. For a released estate it means a copy of the release order. For a house covered by a transfer on death affidavit, it means the recorded affidavit and a death certificate.

The title company also searches for mortgages, judgments and unpaid tax. Because Ohio land sales by fiduciaries follow the statute, a sale that skips the court steps can leave a buyer with a cloud on title. If the file is complicated, a probate attorney in the home county can confirm which documents the closing will need before you accept an offer.

sections.h2: What should an Ohio heir do first?
sections.html:
Begin with whatever decides who may sign, then turn to the house. The probate clerk is the first call.

  • Find the original will and file it with the probate court if no one has.
  • Keep the house insured and secured, and redirect the mail.
  • Ask the recorder whether a transfer on death affidavit exists.
  • Request the current tax bill from the county treasurer.
  • Order the date-of-death appraisal.

An estate that needs to move quickly sometimes sells to a buyer who purchases without repairs or showings. If that fits, compare offers on what the estate keeps after transfer tax, payoffs and costs, since those items apply whichever way the house sells.

faqs.q: Does Ohio have an estate tax in 2026?
faqs.a: No. The Ohio Department of Taxation says the tax was repealed for estates with a 2013 or later date of death, and the House Bill 110 sunset ended collection on property first discovered after December 31, 2021.

faqs.q: Do I need a state tax release to transfer a parent's Ohio house?
faqs.a: No. The Department of Taxation says it no longer requires the ET 12, 13 or 14 release forms. Title and probate steps still apply, so ask the probate court clerk what the estate needs.

faqs.q: Is there a federal estate tax on a modest Ohio estate?
faqs.a: Not at that size. The IRS lists $15,000,000 as the federal basic exclusion amount for 2026 deaths and $13,990,000 for 2025 deaths, and estates under that amount are not required to file Form 706 for that reason.

faqs.q: Can a house pass without full probate in Ohio?
faqs.a: Sometimes. A recorded transfer on death affidavit vests title in the named beneficiary under R.C. 5302.22, and a probate court can release an estate with $35,000 or less in assets under R.C. 2113.03. The probate court can tell you which path fits.

faqs.q: Who pays the county transfer tax when an estate sells in Ohio?
faqs.a: The seller named in the deed. R.C. 322.02 puts the charge on the grantor, payable to the county auditor before the deed reaches the recorder, at a rate each county sets within the thirty-cent cap.
